newsitem.title: USA: GM's Oldsmobile general manager to retire.
newsitem.headline: GM's Oldsmobile general manager to retire.

text.p: John Rock, the outspoken, rough-riding chief of General Motors Corp.'s struggling Oldsmobile Division, will step down at the end of the year, GM said Monday.

Rock, a 60-year-old GM veteran, will retire as Oldsmobile general manager and be replaced by Darwin Clark, currently vice president of sales, marketing and after-market sales for GM Europe, Oldsmobile said.

Rock's departure comes after presiding over 4-1/2 years of turmoil at Oldsmobile that included in continued sales declines and a complete overhaul of the division's product line and marketing strategy.
Known for his cowboy boots, Western-style suits and frank talk about GM's problems, Rock often clashed with the automaker's conservative, dark-suit culture.

In 1992, he opened a news conference aimed at quashing rumours that GM's board planned to kill off the division, he told reporters by saying he was "one pissed-off cowboy" because someone was "trying to shoot my horse."
Although popular with Oldsmobile dealers, The Detroit Free Press reported Monday that he clashed with Ronald Zarrella, GM's marketing chief, who was hired away from Bausch & Lomb Inc. in 1994.
Rock was not available for comment, but he was not pushed out of his job, said Oldsmobile spokesman Peter Ternes.
Under Rock, Oldsmobile introduced the Aurora flagship luxury sedan and changed its focus to attract upscale import car buyers.

In a statement, Zarrella said, "John will be missed at General Motors and his dedicated leadership has played a key role in supporting GM's North American Operations turn around over the past several years."

Oldsmobile, the oldest surviving nameplate in the U.S. auto industry, has been suffering a sales decline since hitting its peak in 1985 with 1.07 million units, as it struggles to attract younger buyers and compete with imports.

Speaking to reporters in September, Rock said he expects the division's sales to fall to 330,000 vehicles in 1997 -- its lowest since 1961 -- from about 340,000 to 350,000 in 1996. Sales this year through September were 256,141, down 14.3 percent.
